---
title: "R6. When something turns out to be wrong"
description: "Revisions, corrections, and what the policy asks you to do about each."
---


Nothing in this playbook prevents an error reaching publication. What decides whether that error
damages trust is what happens next, and for official statistics NHSBSA has already written down
what happens next.

## Revisions and corrections at a glance

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-corrections.qmd >}}

## A revision or a correction

The **NHSBSA Revisions and Corrections Policy** treats these as two different things. A revision is
expected: statistics published as provisional and later finalised, a change of methodology, or the
arrival of further data. A correction is an error.

## The three grades of error

The policy grades errors by what they do to the conclusions, not by how big the number is.

| The error | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Significant**, where the change would contradict the conclusions previously drawn from the data | A prominent alert on the website, corrected as soon as possible, and communicated to users and stakeholders |
| **Minor but significant**, insubstantial but warranting immediate correction in professional judgement | The published release is amended and the revision is clearly identified in it |
| **Minor and insignificant**, where a correction would reasonably be deemed inconsequential | Corrected at the next scheduled release rather than immediately |

## Who decides

Decisions on how to address an error in published statistics are made by the **Lead Official for
Statistics**, in consultation with the National Statistician as appropriate, and the amendment is
published alongside the link to the document. Where an error is known but corrected figures are not
yet available, a note goes on the statistics saying so and making clear the figures are subject to
change.

::: {.callout-note title="If your output is not official statistics" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
The policy binds official and national statistics. The behaviour it describes is worth following
anywhere: say what was wrong, say what it changed, say where the corrected version is, and leave
the original visible rather than replacing it silently.

An analysis that quietly acquires new numbers is indistinguishable from an analysis nobody checked.
:::
